author: Stone Fox Capital
title: AT&T: Dividend Fallacy - AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T)
text:
My constant complaint about investors focused on dividends is the lack of attention to the total return. AT&T ( T ) is a prime example of where investors appear solely focused on the consistent dividend hikes while ignoring what has been a horrible stock this decade. The current 7.2% dividend yield is understandably appealing, but investors shouldn't become fixated on AT&T as a long-term investment due to small dividend hikes.
Image Source: AT&T website
Decade Of Failure Based on just about all data points, AT&T has failed miserably in this decade. Whether comparing the stock to the S&P 500 index or peer Verizon Communications ( VZ ), the returns of AT&T have been horrible.
Compared to the S&P 500 index, AT&T has seen the total return trail that of the market index. The stock has been flat over the last decade while the S&P 500 is up nearly 180%. Over all periods of 1 year, 3 years, 5 years, and 10 years, AT&T has seen depressing total returns in comparison to just holding an index fund and avoiding the single-stock risk of the wireless giant.
Source: Seeking Alpha - Momentum page
When making the cumulative comparison to Verizon since the start of this decade in 2010, the performance is even more depressing. Verizon is up over 81% since the start of 2010 while AT&T has only generated a total return of 66%.
T data by YCharts
Yes, you read that right. An investor in Verizon didn't even need the dividends to exceed the total return of AT&T. Adding in the dividends, Verizon has actually exceeded the gains of the S&P 500 index with a 181% return.
Dividend Obligations My previous research brought out the concept of dividends being obligations that one shouldn't always celebrate. In the case of AT&T, the telecom company has a pattern of just hiking the dividend by ~2% annually.
The stock has gone nowhere this decade despite the quarterly dividend being hiked from $0.41 prior to the start of 2010 to $0.51 now. The quarterly dividend is up 24%.
T data by YCharts
My argument is that these consistent annual dividend hikes are out of touch with the financial prospects of the company defeating the whole purpose of dividends. Remember that AT&T has seen EPS and FCFs surge the last couple of years due to mergers and tax reform as follows:
2017A - EPS = $3.05, FCF = $17.6B 2018E - EPS = $3.52, FCF = $21.0B 2019E - EPS = $3.58, FCF = $26.0B With EPS growth up over $0.50, the annual dividend hike of $0.04 is a warning that the market shouldn't expect the company to grow earnings and cash flows in the future. The company isn't even paying out 10% of the earnings gains via dividends.
For those that question why my research harps on heavy indebted companies constantly hiking dividends, one only needs to look at this chart of General Electric ( GE ). Those dividend hikes became obligations of the company that prevented the industrial giant from paying down debt.
GE data by YCharts
The end result hasn't been pretty for shareholders. The goal of this exercise is to keep AT&T investors from the same fate in the future.
More Obligations The prime issue with big dividend obligations is that AT&T is involved in a highly capital intensive business. Over the last decade, the wireless giant has only maintained flat spending levels on capital expenditures in the $20 billion range.
The interesting aspect here is that tech giants like Alphabet ( GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) and Apple ( AAPL ) are increasingly spending more on capex. Neither company spent much on capex when the decade started and both are in the process of surpassing the wireless giants.
T Capital Expenditures (TTM) data by YCharts
The disconnect here is that AT&T isn't investing for the future as much as hiking capital returns to shareholders. Over this last decade, the dividend payout obligations have surged. Part of the issue is the additional shares from the acquisitions of Time Warner and DirecTV have obligated the company to larger payouts while the capex hasn't grown. The company is spending less on the wireless network in the process.
A very noteworthy point is how Alphabet has ramped up capex, but the company isn't paying dividends while Apple has had a more tepid boost in capex and significantly grown the dividends. Both companies have combined obligations in the mid-$20 billion range, but neither has these obligations plus a large debt load.
T Total Dividends Paid (TTM) data by YCharts
Not All Bad While my research constantly harps on the fallacies of these "mandatory" dividend hikes, my view on the stock remains positive at these levels. With expectations of $26 billion in FCF this year and a dividend obligation of ~$14.85 billion, AT&T currently has plenty of cash to cover the 7%+ dividend and repay debt.
The company set a plan to reach net debt levels of $170 billion at the just-ended quarter and down to ~$150 billion by the end of 2019. The move is simply based on FCF and few small asset sales.
Source: AT&T 2018 Analyst Meeting
Here is where the focus on the total return will pay off. The debt building acquisitions of the last few years have crushed the P/E multiple the market is willing to pay and another year of paying down debt should lead to multiple expansion.
For the stock to just reach the forward P/E ratio of ~11x at the start of 2018, AT&T will trade at nearly $40 by the end of the year. The total return for 2019 could reach a 40.0% capital gain and a 7.2% dividend return for a 47% total return.
T PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts
Takeaway The key investor takeaway is that AT&T is not in a good long-term position with capex spending above $21 billion and dividend obligations approaching $15 billion. Any hiccups in financial expectations will quickly place the wireless and media giant in a tough position.
The quick debt reduction this year will help the stock rally and provide a strong total return for investors. Going forward though, investors need to focus on EPS and FCF expectations and not minimal dividend hikes that haven't rewarded shareholders in the last decade.
Assuming AT&T rallies to $40 by the end of the year, please don't just hold onto the stock because the dividend yield would remain relatively high at 5.2% after another $0.01 quarterly hike. Make sure the business is actually growing to cover the dividend hike before just thinking about the additional cash payout. The additional dividend obligations could eventually sink the wireless and media giant, so the worst investment decision is to blindly own the stock over the next decade due to the dividend fallacy.
